report:
Based on this evidence, the claim is well-supported, not false.

## Findings

Multiple large, high-quality studies consistently show that bystander hands-only (compression-only) CPR improves survival compared with no bystander CPR at all, and performs comparably to conventional CPR with rescue breaths.

**Key evidence:**

1. **Swedish national registry (30-year study, >100,000 OHCA cases)**: Found that bystander CPR—including the rapidly rising share of compression-only CPR—roughly doubled 30-day survival compared with no bystander CPR, and was a major driver of the threefold increase in survival seen over three decades. By recent years, 88% of patients received bystander CPR ([academic.oup.com](https://academic.oup.com/eurheartj/article/43/46/4817/6655575), [pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10665903/)).

2. **Japanese nationwide population-based studies (Hasegawa/SOS-KANTO and related cohorts, hundreds of thousands of cases)**: Compression-only CPR by bystanders was associated with significantly better neurologically favorable survival than no bystander CPR, and outcomes were similar to or better than conventional CPR, especially for adult, cardiac-cause arrests witnessed by laypeople ([ahajournals.org](https://www.ahajournals.org/doi/10.1161/CIRCULATIONAHA.112.109504), [ahajournals.org](https://www.ahajournals.org/doi/10.1161/circulationaha.114.014905)).

3. **Lancet meta-analysis (Hüpfl et al., 2010)** pooling three RCTs and observational data found chest-compression-only CPR associated with improved survival versus standard CPR, both of which greatly exceed outcomes with no CPR ([thelancet.com](https://www.thelancet.com/journals/lancet/article/PIIS0140-6736(10)61454-7/fulltext)).

4. **American Heart Association's 2008 scientific advisory**, based on systematic review of the evidence, concluded hands-only CPR and conventional CPR yield similar survival, and both are far superior to no bystander intervention, which is why AHA recommends hands-only CPR for untrained bystanders ([ahajournals.org](https://www.ahajournals.org/doi/10.1161/circulationaha.107.189380)).

## Conclusion

The claim is accurate and reflects mainstream resuscitation science: bystander hands-only CPR reliably increases survival after out-of-hospital cardiac arrest relative to no CPR, based on converging evidence from national registries (Sweden, Japan), randomized trials, and systematic reviews/meta-analyses spanning over a decade of research.
